content_en:
# Google's Gemini 4 Argon is closer to the AI frontier than any Google model in months

**Google Deepmind is the second major AI lab to pass 95 percent on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark. But the results depend heavily on the testing method, and Argon trails rivals in math and software engineering, according to Epoch AI.**

Google Deepmind's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, scored 97.5 percent on ARC-AGI-3 at a cost of $4,800 using the "Provider Adapter Harness," a test setup that uses vendor-specific features like retained reasoning and context compaction. According to ARC Prize, Google is now the second AI lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark on what is widely considered the toughest benchmark for general problem-solving. Only GPT-6 Astra scores higher at 99.9 percent.

Like Astra, Argon needed 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline across the 25 public games. It matched or beat the speedrun record in three games and came within 10 percent of the best time in six others. On older versions of the benchmark, Argon scored 91.3 percent on ARC-AGI-2 ($0.32 per task) and 98.5 percent on ARC-AGI-1 ($0.16 per task), based on the introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

## Benchmark results depend heavily on the testing setup

In the "Standard Harness," which only allows simple notes between rounds, Argon drops to 49.8 percent at low reasoning for $5,800. This gap traces back to a July 2026 dispute when OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol beat Claude Opus 5 on ARC-AGI-3 using two API settings.

GPT-5.6 Sol only managed 7.8 percent in the standard environment, which discards internal reasoning after each action and used an older interface lacking newer Claude API features. That meant Claude was tested under different conditions than GPT-5.6. When tested with OpenAI's own Responses API, including "Retained Reasoning" and smart context "Compaction," the model jumped to 38.3 percent and beat Opus 5 at 30.2 percent. OpenAI argued that benchmarks always measure the technical environment too. ARC Prize co-founder Francois Chollet then allowed general, publicly available API settings.

API problems also prevented Argon from completing all 55 games in the Standard Harness, according to the testers. At low reasoning, the system finished 42 games (49.8 percent), at medium 46 games (46.3 percent). At the highest level, it only completed 19 games, so ARC Prize did not publish a score. The reported results still cover all 55 games by including partial points from aborted runs.

## Argon closes the gap but lags in math and coding

Research institute Epoch AI tracked Google's progress too. Argon scored 165 points on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), tying Fable 5.1 and landing just behind Opus 5.5 (167) and GPT-6 Astra (166). The ECI combines over 50 benchmarks into a single capability scale, similar to how Artificial Analysis builds its main score.

Argon jumps well ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (157 points) and brings Google closer to the top than at any point since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February. Artificial Analysis and Vals.ai confirmed this trend before.

Performance varies by domain, though. According to Epoch AI, Argon leads several knowledge, agent, and vision benchmarks, but early estimates put it in eighth on the Math ECI and sixth on the Software Engineering Index (SWE ECI).

content_en:
# China plans to tighten export controls on open-weight models and 23 key AI technologies

## Key Points

- China's commerce and science ministries are moving to tighten AI export controls, releasing a draft rule that targets 23 key areas including frontier models, AI agents, and autonomous malware tools.
- Model restrictions kick in if a system was trained on sensitive Chinese data, or if it hits 2 trillion parameters, 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, or a global top-10 ranking.
- To keep from slowing down domestic AI labs, the plan fast-tracks open-weight releases with automatic approval upon registration. Any AI tech that is already public is completely exempt.

**China's commerce and science ministries have released a draft update to the nation's list of banned and restricted export technologies.**

The catalog targets 23 key AI technologies across large models, agents, compute clusters, and data processing. AI tools that can write or alter malware on their own to attack critical infrastructure, the military, or government agencies face a total export ban. Certain AI tools for finding software vulnerabilities won't be banned outright, though they will face new export limits.

Large AI models also face export controls in two cases. The first covers models trained on China's "important data" (as defined by the country's Data Security Law and related rules) that offer services based on it. Lawfully public data is exempt. Tiny amounts of up to 0.1 percent are also allowed if the data was cleaned beforehand, never shows up in AI outputs, and doesn't substantially boost the model's R&D capacity for core tech in that field.

The second case covers the core technologies behind large models, including weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training or inference methods. These controls kick in once a model hits 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, has at least 2 trillion parameters, or ranks in the global top 10. Export officials determine that top-10 status using public rankings from major domestic and foreign evaluators or industry platforms, looking at overall performance, specific tasks, safety, or global usage numbers.

"This move does not mean 'China is shutting down open-weight models,' but it does indicate the Chinese government establishing the optionality to shut down future open-weight models at will," writes Dean W. Ball, head of strategic futures at OpenAI. Ball adds that Beijing's framework is a "mirror image" of the model-weight export controls the US government has already put in place.

This will likely push US companies that rely on open-weight AI to double down on domestic models instead of Chinese alternatives. Europe is in a much tougher spot. The EU has been banking on running open-weight models in domestic clouds to stay independent, alongside companies that want to host closed top-tier models on local servers. That sovereignty strategy falls apart when all the best open models come from the US or China and can get cut off by export controls at any time. At least AI tech that is already public through open-source releases or research papers skips these new rules entirely.

## Fast-track rules protect China's open-source boom while restricting local foreign deployments

To avoid choking off its domestic open-source boom, China is introducing a fast-track process at the same time. Publishing restricted AI tech and weights as open source qualifies for "automatic licensing." The same goes for Chinese firms that run their own data centers abroad, tape out chips overseas, conduct research with foreign partners, or help set international standards. Under the ministry's rules, eligible exports are cleared the moment a company files the paperwork.

Using restricted models through API calls, apps, websites, SaaS tools, or lightweight versions on local devices stays free of these export controls. Installing restricted AI tech on local servers abroad, however, requires a standard export license. Companies can still use the streamlined process if the software runs on their own overseas cloud.

Beijing also pledges to back AI development in the Global South and ease exports for capacity building, tech sharing, and joint rulemaking within the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, a bloc China launched to counter Western AI bodies. Until the final rules take effect, companies must register affected exports through the commerce ministry's portal.

title_en: Physical AI is more than robots, says the Nvidia veteran now investing in it
excerpt_en: Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA’s robotics platforms, says robotics is currently in its “Lego era,” with the basic building blocks like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt. This view runs counter to those who believe that robotics, powered by a general foundation model, is about to have […]
content_en:
Amulya Vishwanath, who spent seven years leading product marketing for NVIDIA’s robotics platforms, says robotics is currently in its “Lego era,” with the basic building blocks like actuators, robotic hands, software, and safety standards still being rebuilt.

This view runs counter to those who believe that robotics, powered by a general foundation model, is about to have its “ChatGPT moment” — that day when the shockingly capable chatbot was launched in late 2022. (General Intuition CEO Pim de Witte told Equity earlier this year that a single general foundation model would make much of today’s specialized robotics work redundant, and be that moment.)

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Dominic-Madori Davis caught up with Vishwanath to discuss where she’s writing first checks as the founder and managing partner of Techable VC. They also talked about what she’s learned as one of the first women executives to spin out of Nvidia and launch her own early-stage firm investing in physical AI across robotics, materials science, and life sciences.

Listen to the full episode to hear more about:

- Why Vishwanath defines physical AI as more than robots: “a molecule, a material, a medicine,” or a machine on a factory line.

- What she means by “conscious automation.”

- Why the best opportunities solve big problems like family-run factories that can’t find workers to surgeons facing burnout.

- Why she wants founders to see their VC as their moat, and how years at NVIDIA built the network she now uses for due diligence and customer introductions.

- Where she thinks the U.S. and China each have the edge, and why humanoids should be good for more than dancing.

content_en:
# ChatGPT becomes a full Chrome browser assistant that reads and acts on your open tabs

**ChatGPT can now access open tabs right in the Chrome browser and take actions on them.** Users can target open tabs with `@chrome`, while Chat mode pulls data from several tabs at once. Work mode lets the tool control tabs through Computer Use to send messages, fill out forms, download files, or group tabs. GPT-6 Astra is the best Computer Use model on the market right now, and it can handle complex workflows with many steps.

Your full chat history now sits in the upgraded ChatGPT sidebar right next to the web page you're viewing. In OpenAI's examples, the extension compares products across open tabs by size, material, shipping time, and return rules, sums up articles in plain language, or matches up price pages from different sellers. The updated Chrome extension works with all ChatGPT plans.

title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Spending Contracts For Latest AI-Driven Startup Batch
excerpt: Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions.
title_en: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: Spending Contracts For Latest AI-Driven Startup Batch
excerpt_en: Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions.
content_en:
*Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board.*

*This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here.*

Startup investors aren’t exactly hitting pause, but they did scale back on giant rounds this past week, with just two startup financings in the multiple hundreds of millions. The biggest round went to AI infrastructure provider Modal Labs, which picked up $750 million, followed by construction automation unicorn Icon, which secured $200 million. Other sectors that attracted larger rounds this past week included biotech, insurance and AI.

1\. **Modal Labs, $750M, AI infrastructure:** Modal Labs, a provider of cloud infrastructure for AI inference and other applications, secured $750 million in a Series D funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation. The New York-headquartered company said it recently exceeded an annual revenue run rate of $1 billion.

2\. **Icon, $200M, construction tech:** Austin-based Icon, a developer of robotic construction systems known for its 3D-printed homes, closed on $200 million in Series D funding led by  Baillie Gifford and BlackRock. The company says it is on pace for 4x revenue growth in 2026.

3\. **Soufflé Therapeutics, $135M, RNA therapies:** Boston-based Soufflé Therapeutics, a developer of RNA therapies, raised $135 million in Series B funding led by Juvia Group as part of a large syndicate of investors.

4\. **Estuary Biotherapeutics, $103M, gene therapies:** Menlo Park, California-based Estuary Biotherapeutics, a developer of genetic medicines for patients with serious kidney diseases, launched with $103 million in financing. The funding includes $93 million in a Series A round led by RA Capital Management as well as $10 million in previously undisclosed seed capital.

5\. **Labelbox, $100M, AI tools:** Labelbox, a developer of technology to train and evaluate AI models and to help deploy agents that improve with experience, picked up $100 million in Series E funding. Infinitum Partners led the financing for the 8-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

6\. **Suki, $90M, health AI:** Redwood City, California-based Suki, a provider of AI tools that turn clinical conversations into intelligence for documentation, coding and other healthcare workflows, announced a $90 million Series E financing from backers including Healthier Capital and Crosslink Capital.

7\. **Abby Care, $82M, caregiver platform:** Abby Care, a platform for family members to become certified, paid caregivers and deliver care at home, closed on $82 million in Series C funding, per a Fortune report. Transformation Capital led the financing for the 5-year-old, San Francisco-based startup.

8\. **Stand, $70M, insurance:** Stand, a provider of insurance for homes in areas at higher risk of natural disasters, secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation. Saga Ventures led the financing for the 3-year-old, San Francisco-based company.

9\. **Mueon, $65M, semiconductor systems:** Mueon Corp., a semiconductor systems company building a modular platform for AI and hyperscale computing, completed a $65 million Series A funding round. Maverick Silicon led the financing for the Portland, Oregon-based company.

10\. **North.cloud, $60M, AI spend management:** New York-based North.cloud, provider of an infrastructure spend intelligence and automation platform, raised $60 million in a Series B round led by PeakSpan Capital.

## Methodology

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 10-16, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

*Illustration: Dom Guzman*

Stay up to date with recent funding rounds, acquisitions, and more with the Crunchbase Daily.

content_en:
Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models.

# A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops

Nvidia’s new Arm-based laptop chip is an exciting new challenger, but exclusively for the high-end.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing.

All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM.

These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s *a lot* to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week.

Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep?

## Does it just work?

**Antonio Di Benedetto:** Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer.

Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities.

**Sean Hollister:** Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode.

But I largely agree with Antonio. I made an RTX Spark my daily driver, with all my typical work and personal apps — Signal, Discord, Audacity, CapCut and Evernote, Irfanview, Slack, ScreenToGif and more — and nothing has failed me so far. I never once needed to think whether I was running an Arm or an x86 app. The real hitches came with gaming and AI, as you’ll read below.

**Tom Warren:** I’ve been using a Windows on Arm laptop with a Qualcomm chip daily for the past two years and things have improved to the point that I can’t tell if an app is native or not anymore. That’s the same story on the RTX Spark laptops, and I feel like Nvidia’s entry into this category will only improve the story for creative apps and gaming.

## Can it game?

**TW:** Windows on Arm never looked like a serious gaming platform before now. While there still aren’t many native Arm games, Nvidia’s GPU helps bruteforce through the emulation layer. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games.

I mostly game on my desktop, where I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. I was able to run *Black Myth: Wukong* at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in *Cyberpunk 2077* and averaged 66fps, and *Forza Horizon 6* managed an average of 57fps.

In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.

**SH:** Like Tom says, the GPU power is there — but the CPU might hold back some of your games. I had plenty of power for a smooth 60fps in *Returnal* (at 1440p with high settings), *Expedition 33* (at a DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with high settings), *Jedi Survivor* (DLSS “Performance” upscaled 1200p with medium settings), and *Shadow of the Tomb Raider* (at native 1800p and highest spec).

But when I fired up *Helldivers 2*, even dipping down to a DLSS-upscaled 1080p was no guarantee of 60fps in the highest difficulty missions. There are just too many enemies on screen for the Spark to keep up. *Star Wars Zero Company* is even more CPU-bound *—* the Spark didn’t care whether I was maximizing or minimizing the graphics and screen resolution. No matter what I tried, I typically saw my framerate capped between 37fps and 39fps in battle.

Even ancient and low-powered games can have quirks. I tried the 2003 title *Max Payne 2* and saw situations where framerate dipped to 50fps. I even saw a few hitches in the excellent *UFO 50*, a collection of 2D games, though a couple other 2D games ran great.

I’m also not sure if RTX Spark is suitable for VR yet. The excellent *Titanfall 2* VR mod worked, and it seemed to run fine at first, but lost a little stability after a few minutes. That could be my Wi-Fi, because the driver for Valve’s Steam Frame wireless adapter wouldn’t install on the Spark. Neither did Steam’s streaming audio solution, so the audio came out of the Nvidia laptop instead of the headset.

Just so we’re clear, all of this is assuming you want a laptop maxing out its fans and positively dumping heat on your desk or lap. That’s not unusual for thin gaming notebooks, but it’s *way* louder and hotter than a good desktop or handheld.

**AD:** I’ve wanted a MacBook Pro-like laptop with full PC gaming chops for as long as I can remember, so I was hyped for these laptops to deliver the goods in graphics. The first night, I set up the Asus ProArt P16, with all 128GB of its ridiculously large pool of memory, and when I booted up *Big Walk* for my planned online evening with some friends my first thought was, “Well, that looks okay. I guess.” I know *Big Walk* isn’t some triple-A graphical titan, but it has some fairly demanding graphics for the “friend slop” genre. I expected the N1X to max it out, or at least get close, but not really.

I had to bump the P16’s 4K display down to 2560 x 1600, and instead of *Big Walk’s* Highest or Very high graphics presets, I brought it down to High to maintain a decently solid 60-ish fps. Does any of that really matter for this silly co-op game about solving puzzles with your buddies? Of course not. It looked fine, after all. But it was a sobering reminder that this “superchip” is no graphical magician.

title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
excerpt: The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles.
title_en: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
excerpt_en: The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles.
content_en:
AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.”

The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”

This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.

At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.

CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.

For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.

In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

content_en:
### Physics AI pushes chip design beyond traditional simulation

Vinci4D Inc. is bringing a new approach to semiconductor design grounded in fundamental physics equations.

The company provides simulation software for chip designers, offering an alternative to traditional simulation methods, including finite element analysis, a technique engineers use to study the physical behavior of objects. Instead, Vinci4D’s technology uses pretrained physics models to accelerate simulations and analyze multiple physical phenomena simultaneously.

“Vinci is changing how design and analysis is being done from the ground up,” said Karthik Aravamudhan (pictured), global client director at Vinci4D. “The whole industry is talking about agentic AI and how the workflow automation, the orchestration, happens. That means more simulations, more analysis, a lot more that needs to happen under the hood. Vinci is trying to attack that problem.”

Aravamudhan spoke with theCUBE’s Christophe Bertrand at SEMICON West, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed Vinci’s approach to physics-based simulation and its implications for semiconductor design and agentic AI. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Physics foundation models reshape semiconductor design

Physics foundation models could play a growing role in semiconductor engineering, according to Aravamudhan. He highlighted the strategic shift from Design Technology Co-Optimization to System Technology Co-Optimization, which involves thinking of chip design as one part of a larger system.

“\[Vinci\] fundamentally tries to solve the problem from the foundational physics level,” Aravamudhan said. “When you’re designing, you’re trying to understand what the package looks like. While you’re designing the package, you’re trying to understand what the board looks like. So, you’re designing a whole system; you’re not just designing one portion of it anymore.”

Vinci trains its models on physics equations rather than customer data, reducing the need to expose proprietary design information during model training. Its technology also aims to reduce the time and cost of simulations by analyzing multiple physical phenomena simultaneously.

“An average customer today in the whole semiconductor ecosystem tries to solve for a certain physics,” Aravamudhan explained. “It could be thermal, it can be mechanical and it can by any\[thing\]. They try to solve one physics at a time because that’s the only way it has been known to be possible. That takes a whole long time. What Vinci tries to do with these foundational physics models is try to solve these physics true to what it is and to solve multiple of these at the same time.”

Vinci recently closed a $250 million Series B funding round at a $1.5 billion valuation, co-led by Advent International, Temasek and Xora. The startup now plans to expand its reach beyond semiconductors into other hardware industries, including automotive and aerospace applications.

“The funding gives us … the foundation to go after bigger \[things\],” Aravamudhan said. “From the different physics that we can solve, from having a go-to-market team and a go-to-market approach, it gives us so many different dimensions we can start focusing on. With these big names backing us, it certainly helps a lot and it shows their belief not only in Vinci, but their belief in the technology.”

content_en:
### Knowledge graphs fuel AI innovation for financial services at Raymond James Financial

Knowledge graphs are becoming a critical context and reasoning layer for agentic AI, helping enterprises connect data and ground agents in key areas of business expertise.

For diversified financial services companies such as Raymond James Financial Inc., graph technologies have become an important part of developing trustworthy infrastructure to support AI. The technology has been particularly helpful in building unique solutions, according to Jeff Griffith (pictured, left), vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James.

“Using something like a data graph lets us harness the power of AI in dynamic ways,” Griffith said. “People already know how to go get the things that they’re getting every day. But it’s when you want to cross those domains or do some unique thing that this has a lot of value.”

Griffith spoke with John Furrier, executive analyst for theCUBE Research, at the recent GraphSummit event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. He was joined by Naveen Mahankali (right), vice president of technology at Raymond James, and they discussed how knowledge graphs and AI are changing the business landscape. *(\* Disclosure below.)*

### Knowledge graphs for data reliability

As a Neo4j customer, Raymond James uses graph technologies that give developers a way to represent the relationships, dependencies and business context that AI applications need to reason effectively. Accuracy is a critical requirement in the financial world, and Raymond James uses its knowledge graph to help agents work with data from trusted systems and evaluate results against established sources.

“We have golden sources, we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” Mahankali told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”

Raymond James’ work with AI is creating new efficiencies within the organization. Looking ahead, Mahankali sees opportunities for AI to reduce the time and effort financial advisors spend sourcing information for clients.

“One of the things we’re trying to do is we’re letting AI query the data dynamically so that our financial advisors get what they want without clicking on screens and without looking at a fixed dashboard,” he said. “They can do more analysis rather than just looking at the data that they already see in other applications. They can do product analysis versus how accounts are balanced and things like that by asking a question.”

The implementation of AI agents is also changing everyday processes within Raymond James itself. In January, the company launched Raimond, its proprietary digital AI operations agent.

“We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith said. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people, how everyone works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”

title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
excerpt: According to Elorian's evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
title_en: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
excerpt_en: According to Elorian's evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
content_en:
Elorian, the Palo Alto AI startup that raised a $55 million seed round at a $300 million valuation before it launched a product, released its first model on Friday, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

The model, Glimpse, is launching as a research preview with API access and a chat interface is waitlist-only, so for now it’s a results table and a thesis. The thesis? Today’s AI models, for all their skill with language and code, still can’t really see.

Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.

For former Google DeepMind researcher and Elorian CEO Andrew Dai, one of the clearest signs that AI still couldn’t really see came on game night.

Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say. Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”

“Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right? Why can’t AI models?” he said.

The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply. The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against.

Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.

But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.

Elorian came out of stealth six months ago with a round co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures, and Altimeter Capital, with participation from Nvidia and Google chief scientist Jeff Dean.

The initial targets are companies sitting on lots of video: robotics firms, scientific labs, media, and creative companies. Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing. That means building a model of a scene using that to choose an action, including directly controlling robots. Next year, Dai said, the company aims to build “the world’s best visual reasoning model,” one that leads on every visual reasoning test.

title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
excerpt: The data comes from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.
title_en: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
excerpt_en: The data comes from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.
content_en:
Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.

Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.

Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon, among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.

The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.

The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend.

While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be complementary rather than competitive.

title: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
excerpt: Actor and angel investor Mark Wahlberg says he's OK with using AI in filmmaking, provided it's used "to enhance what you're doing."
title_en: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
excerpt_en: Actor and angel investor Mark Wahlberg says he's OK with using AI in filmmaking, provided it's used "to enhance what you're doing."
content_en:
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.

The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing \[AI\] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”

That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.

“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault, a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”

He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life \[…\] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”

content_en:
### AI safety worries multiply but everyone’s still racing full speed ahead

The drumbeat over how safe artificial intelligence is — or more to the point, isn’t — just keeps louder.

In the wake of weeks of incidents involving rogue agents, with likely more to come, more government officials are calling for regulation, even if President Trump says it’s not needed. Several states are suing OpenAI over harms to kids. And even many people in tech are calling for more controls, including several hundred AI researchers worried about cybersecurity issues and Microsoft President Brad Smith, who says AI is less regulated than a carton of milk.

One big issue: Who gets to say any particular AI is safe? That’s the question Dave Vellante explored in his latest Breaking Analysis. He concluded that “we should advance the evidence and engineering for control alongside the capability of the models. For policymakers, that means an independent standard with consequences. For businesses, it means granting more authority only when the deployment earns trust.” Indeed, for some companies, AI agents in particular just may not be the answer at all, wrote Intellyx’s Jason Bloomberg.

Meanwhile, investors are starting to vote with their dollars on AI, increasingly worried that revenue growth for AI, namely for leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic, might not continue as fast as it has this year. Though Anthropic revealed to investors 45% revenue growth from the second to the third quarter, that constituted a slowdown, which could bring its planned public offering valuation from $2 trillion to a slightly less incredible $1.5 trillion. And investors had more to worry about, namely CoreWeave’s debt load, which knocked down the stocks of neoclouds and their suppliers this week.

And it’s not just public investors who are getting antsy. As Intel’s and Broadcom’s CEOs pointed out this week, capital is becoming a brake on expansion for AI, especially as interest rates keep creeping up.

Nonetheless, AI companies from Nvidia to Meta are forging ahead with new models. In particular, they’re increasingly offering open-source or open-weight models as enterprises aim to create customized models for their businesses. Look for SiliconANGLE to explore that realm of AI soon.

And the AI picks-and-shovels crowd isn’t slowing down either. At the Open Compute Project’s Summit in San Jose this week, Cisco Systems, Nvidia, Intel and many other suppliers debuted technologies to enable AI to scale up, out and across faster.

Tech earnings season gets underway next week. Besides Netflix and Tesla, there’s IBM, Meta, SAP and more, setting the table for the big cloud/AI players Alphabet and Microsoft the following week.
